title: Jonah
subtitle: the prophet who ran from mercy
lead: Jonah is the shortest story in the Book of the Twelve and the strangest. God tells the prophet Jonah son of Amittai to call out against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, because of its wickedness. Jonah runs the other way, by ship, until the LORD hurls a storm at the sea. The foreign sailors pray and spare him; he is swallowed by a huge fish, prays a psalm of thanks, and is put on dry land. He goes to Nineveh and says five Hebrew words. The whole city, king and animals included, fasts and turns back, and God changes his mind about the harm.

Then Jonah is furious. He tells God he ran because he knew God would forgive. A plant, a worm and a hot wind teach him a lesson, and the book ends with God's question: should I not have pity on Nineveh? The book never says whether Jonah answers. That open ending is part of the point. The reader is left standing where Jonah stands.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a). The story is told about Jonah, not by him, and most scholars think the author is unknown.
Set in the 700s BC, in the days of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). Most scholars think it was written much later, in the Persian period (500s-300s BC); some defend an earlier date.
Joppa, the Mediterranean Sea, and Nineveh, capital of Assyria
Narrative prose with a psalm of thanks (2:2-9). Whether it is history, a parable, a satire or a legend is debated (see "What kind of book is this?").
Hebrew, with a few words that look late or borrowed (for example "ship" in 1:5 and "decree" in 3:7).
English 1:17 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1-10 is Hebrew 2:2-11. Hebrew chapter 1 therefore has 16 verses, chapter 2 has 11. This site uses the English numbers.
The fifth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah...); sixth in the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum...).
authorship: Jewish tradition counts Jonah son of Amittai as the prophet of the story and has the Men of the Great Assembly write the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a). Many traditional Christian writers have held that Jonah himself wrote it.

The book is anonymous and the story is told in the third person about a man of the 700s BC. Most critics date it between 500 and 200 BC, from late vocabulary, from the use of Exodus 34:6 and Joel 2:13 (4:2), from the phrase "God of the heavens" (1:9), and from "Nineveh was a city great in God's eyes" (3:3), which looks back on a city that no longer stands.
Stuart and Alexander argue that none of these features rules out the 700s BC, and hold that Jonah or a contemporary wrote it. Their commentaries are cited in the notes.

audience.to: Judeans of the Persian period (the 400s-300s BC) are the most likely first readers: a small community in Yehud, back from exile, living under foreign rule with the memory of Assyria's and Babylon's violence. The book is set in the 700s and names Nineveh, a city that was destroyed in 612 BC. Others place it much earlier, for the northern kingdom in Jeroboam II's day, or much later.
audience.why: To ask what Israel does with a God who is merciful to its enemies. The book gives no sermon: it tells a story in which the prophet runs from the job, foreigners understand God's reach better than he does, the worst city on earth turns back at five words, and the prophet is angry at the result. The question at the end is for the reader. Knowing the audience changes the reading: for Persian-period Judeans, "Nineveh" stands for every empire that had harmed them, and Jonah's anger is the anger they felt. The book asks whether they would be right to feel it.
views: The northern kingdom in the 700s BC
Stuart and Alexander: the book was written for Israel, under threat from Assyria, and warns that God will show mercy to Assyria if it repents, and judgment to Israel if it does not.

The common critical view (Sasson, Limburg, Wolff): the story is a late, instructive tale for a community that had to live with the empires that ruled it. The use of Exodus 34:6 and Joel 2:13 in 4:2 and the Jewish Yom Kippur reading both fit this.
A Jewish teaching on repentance, read yearly

In Jewish practice the book is read on Yom Kippur afternoon (Bavli Megillah 31a). In this use its first audience is every Jew that day: the question is how God receives repentance, and how people should feel about it.

outline: The call to Nineveh and Jonah's flight
The storm, the lot, the sailors' prayers and Jonah thrown overboard
The huge fish and Jonah's psalm of thanks
The second call; Nineveh believes, fasts and turns back; God changes his mind
The plant, the worm, the wind, and God's closing question

lenses.name: History
lenses.desc: Reads the book against the 700s BC and the Assyrian world: Jonah of Gath-hepher in Jeroboam II's day (2 Kings 14:25), Nineveh, Assyria's cruelty and its later fall, Tarshish. It asks what can be known and what cannot, including what the Assyrian eponym lists record (a plague and an eclipse, which no text links to Jonah).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks when and why the book was written, whether the psalm in 2:2-9 belongs to it, what its borrowings from Exodus 34:6, Joel 2:13 and the Psalms show, how it relates to Nahum, and what sea-monster stories elsewhere tell us (little).

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Jonah as Jews have read it: the Yom Kippur afternoon reading (with the Micah passage many communities add), Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimhi, the Targum, the Mekhilta and the midrash on the fish and on Jonah's flight.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Jonah as the church has: the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:38-42; 16:4; Luke 11:29-32), the fathers' typology (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Jerome, Augustine), the mission to the nations (Acts 10; Matthew 28:19), Jonah in early Christian art, and the reading of Jonah as narrow-minded Israel, which this site corrects.

lenses.name: Literary and genre
lenses.desc: Reads the book as a made thing: its genre (historical report, parable, satire, didactic story, legend), irony, repetition, reversal and open ending. This lens takes the place of the usual "Still to come" lens (F), which is dropped on purpose: Jonah looks back on a finished event, and the question is how the reader takes the story, not what it predicts.

sections.b:
Jonah tells a story, and it tells it with a small set of repeated words. Reading it as a collection of oracles will not work. Watch for these, which the notes name at first use: gadol, "great" (the great city, wind, storm, fear and fish, Jonah's "great evil," and the great joy of 4:6); ra'ah, "evil" or "disaster" or "harm" (1:2; 1:7-8; 3:8, 10; 4:1-2, 6); yarad, "go down" (1:3, 5; 2:6); tul, "hurl" (1:4, 5, 12, 15); yare', "fear" (1:5, 9, 10, 16); nicham, "change one's mind" (3:9, 10; 4:2), the same English the site uses in Jeremiah and Joel; and manah, "appoint" (1:17; 4:6, 7, 8). The Plain English Translation keeps the repetition visible where English can, and the notes say where it cannot.

The story has two halves that mirror each other. In the first, God commands, the prophet flees, foreigners pray, and a psalm is prayed from the deep. In the second, God commands, the prophet obeys, foreigners repent, and Jonah prays an angry prayer under a plant. The story ends with a question God asks the prophet, and so the reader.

English verse numbers differ from Hebrew at 1:17 (Hebrew 2:1) and in chapter 2 (English 2:1-10 = Hebrew 2:2-11). The Greek (Swete's text) follows the Hebrew numbering. This site gives English numbers throughout.

The base text is the Leningrad Codex. The Greek is read in Swete's edition, which prints mainly Codex Vaticanus. The critical editions (Rahlfs and Hanhart; the Göttingen Duodecim Prophetae) were not consulted, so "the Greek" in this book means Swete's text and not the reconstructed Old Greek. The Dead Sea Scroll transcriptions are read as well (Abegg, Bowley and Cook; Qumran scrolls 4QXIIa, 4Q76; 4QXIIf, 4Q81; 4QXIIg, 4Q82; and the Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve, Mur88). The scrolls preserve parts of all four chapters and agree with the Masoretic Text in meaning wherever the transcription is not restored; they differ in spelling, in 4Q76 and 4Q82's fuller vowel letters, and in a few small readings listed in the variants. Some smaller forms are not listed one by one and change no sense: 4Q76 spells Joppa as יפא (1:3) and has לים for אל הים (1:5); 4Q82 has כעלות for בעלות (4:7); Mur88 has על for אל before God (3:8). The notable differences are in the Greek: "servant of the Lord" for "Hebrew" (1:9), "the cry of" added in 1:2, "three days" for "forty" (3:4), "gourd" for the plant (4:6), "to shade him" for "to rescue him" (4:6, shared with a spelling in 4Q82), and a run of shifts in the psalm (2:4-9). Jerome's Vulgate follows the Hebrew and is the witness for "ivy." The Targum and Peshitta are later and are not used as sources for the Plain English Translation.

The story is set in the days of Jeroboam II (about 793-753 BC), but most critical scholars think it was written much later, in the Persian period. The reasons are the use of Exodus 34:6-7 and Joel 2:13 in 4:2, the phrase "God of the heavens" (1:9), late words such as the ones for "ship" and "decree," the past tense of "Nineveh was a city great in God's eyes" (3:3). Stuart and Alexander defend the 700s BC, and say that the language and the creed do not require a late writer. The psalm (2:2-9) is thought by some to be an insertion (Wolff) and by others to belong to the book's irony (Landes, Magonet, Sasson, Trible). The comparison with the stories of sea monsters swallowing heroes in Mesopotamia and Greece is weak. The closest is the Greek story of Heracles, swallowed by the sea monster of Hesione's tale, who spends three days inside and comes out bald (Lycophron, Alexandra, and later writers); it shares the shape and the three days, but it is late, it has no prophet or repentance, and it makes a different point. None shares both the shape and the point of Jonah's story, and the Hebrew does not use a monster word (dag gadol is simply "a great fish").

sections.h: What kind of book is this?
sections.b: Five views are held, and none is the settled one. (1) History: a report about a real prophet (2 Kings 14:25), held by the early church and by many conservatives today (Stuart, Alexander). (2) Parable or didactic story: a made-up tale told to teach, like Jesus's parables. (3) Satire: a comic exaggeration that ridicules an unwilling prophet and narrow-mindedness. (4) Legend: a story grown from a prophet's memory. (5) A mixture: a core of history shaped into a story. Commentators who read the book as a crafted story, not a strict report, include Wolff, Sasson, Trible, Limburg, Simon, Ben Zvi and Magonet, each with a different label; Stuart and Alexander defend it as history. The genre does not settle what the book means: all five readings agree that its point is God's concern for Nineveh. Jesus's use of Jonah in Matthew 12:41 is used on both sides: some say he treats it as history, others that he uses a story as an illustration, as he does with the good Samaritan.

The whole book is read on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, at the afternoon (minchah) service (Bavli Megillah 31a). Many communities then add Micah 7:18-20, a later custom. The reading casts Nineveh's repentance as the model and God's pardon as the answer, and the prayer in the psalm echoes the day's themes. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Kimhi (Radak) wrote commentaries on it, and the Targum of the Prophets paraphrases it in Aramaic. Rashi and the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael say Jonah ran because he feared Gentile repentance would shame Israel. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer (about AD 750-850) and Genesis Rabbah (about AD 400-500) preserve later legends: the fish was made at creation; Jonah saw wonders inside it; the sailors became converts. These are legends, not readings of the Hebrew.

Jesus gave "the sign of Jonah" to those who asked for a sign (Matthew 12:38-42; 16:4; Luke 11:29-32). Matthew explains it by the three days in the fish and the three days in the earth; Luke by Jonah's preaching. From Justin Martyr on, the fathers read the fish as the tomb and Jonah's rescue as the resurrection; Jerome wrote a commentary on it; Augustine wrote on it in letters (71 and 82) and in the City of God (18.30 and 18.44), and he and Jerome argued over the plant. Jonah is one of the most common subjects in the early Christian art of the catacombs and sarcophagi, in the cycle of the sailors throwing him in, the monster, and his rest under the plant (Jensen, Understanding Early Christian Art). Luther and Calvin lectured on it. Churches of the East keep a Fast of Nineveh before Lent. Many preachers read Jonah as "Israel" and the book as a rebuke of Jewish exclusiveness, a reading that the book itself does not support and that this site corrects. The book's own point is rather the mercy that reaches the nations (Acts 10:34-35; Matthew 28:19).

sections.h: Where Jonah sits among the Twelve
sections.b: The Hebrew Bible counts the Twelve as one scroll (Sirach 49:10; Bava Batra 13b-15a). The Masoretic order puts Jonah after Obadiah; the Greek puts it after Obadiah too, but moves Joel and Micah to stand earlier. The Twelve link in several places: Joel 2:13-14 and Jonah 3:9; 4:2 share the creed and the "Who knows?"; Obadiah's judgment on Edom is followed by a book about mercy to Assyria; in the Masoretic order Nahum, two books later (after Micah), announces Nineveh's fall, as if answering Jonah; in the Greek order Nahum follows Jonah directly. Whether the Twelve was shaped as one book (Nogalski, Schart, Sweeney) or is simply twelve books on one scroll (Ben Zvi, Barton) is debated. It is not a consensus.

Josephus (Antiquities 9.10.2) retells Jonah's story and says a ketos swallowed him. 3 Maccabees 6:8 (accepted in the Orthodox canon) names Jonah wasting in the belly of the sea monster. Manuscripts of Tobit 14:4 differ on whether it was Jonah or Nahum who foretold Nineveh's fall. The Lives of the Prophets, an early Jewish-Christian work whose date and text are debated, has an entry on Jonah; it is a witness to legend, not a source for the Plain English Translation.

spec.title: Jonah as a reversal of Elijah
spec.body: Jonah's wish to die under a shelter in 4:3 and 4:8 is close to Elijah's under the broom bush (1 Kings 19:4), and both prophets are answered by questions. But Elijah, who has been zealous, is sent back with work to do; Jonah, who has succeeded, gets a question and no instructions. My theory is that the author wrote 4:1-11 as a deliberate turn of the Elijah story: a prophet whose success is worse to him than failure. This overlaps with commentators who note the echo of 1 Kings 19 (Trible, Sasson); the idea of a deliberate reversal is my own labeled reading.

prompts: The storm and the sleeping prophet

A hand-drawn scroll illustration, ink and soft color, of a small wooden ship tossed by a great wind on dark waves; sailors with different gods clutch figures and bags of cargo, and below deck a man lies asleep. Edges soft and torn like old parchment, with cave-drawing figures and a few Hebrew letters in the margins.

A sketch on aged papyrus in the style of an early Christian catacomb painting mixed with modern line art: a man thrown from a ship, a huge curling fish with a gentle eye, and the same man resting under a leafy vine. Soft, uneven borders, no hard rectangle.

A hand-drawn picture of a walled city with towers and winged-bull gates; people, a king and sheep and cattle in rough sackcloth with ash on their heads. Ancient manuscript look, ink and earth colors, edges faded like a scroll.
reading: The fullest commentary: every word, every parallel, and a detailed argument for how the book is built.
Phyllis Trible, Rhetorical Criticism: Context, Method, and the Book of Jonah (1994)
A close reading of the Hebrew's repetition and irony.
A clear commentary for readers who want the history of interpretation.
A Jewish commentary that draws on the medieval rabbis.
Jonathan Magonet, Form and Meaning (1976; 2nd ed. 1983)
The classic study of the book's literary structure.
Ehud Ben Zvi, Signs of Jonah (2003)
On the book as a text read and reread in the Persian period.
